Each removed sentence hooks backwards by reference (that, he, this, such objects, the news, its) and forwards to the next sentence (each repaired, word had spread, a child's bicycle for example, Marsh's comment, those who gave money, she says). The extra sentence (E) tempts gap 4, straight after the badly mended chair and glasses, but it contradicts paragraph 2: Marsh spent thirty-five years repairing televisions. title: The museum of mending
subtitle: Nothing in this small museum is valuable, and everything in it has been broken. Its founder thinks that is exactly the point.
text: In a narrow street behind the market in the small town of Haddleford, there is a museum with no paintings, no fossils and nothing that would interest a thief. Every one of its four hundred objects is broken, or rather, was broken once. {1} The teapot with a silver-wire handle, the doll with one glass eye and one button eye, the umbrella held together with fishing line: each was repaired by someone who could easily have thrown it away and bought another.

The museum's founder, Edwin Marsh, spent thirty-five years repairing televisions before he retired. In all that time, he says, he never once told a customer that a set was not worth fixing. He started the collection almost by accident. {2} Within a few months word had spread, and strangers began leaving parcels on his doorstep, with notes explaining who had mended what, and why.

Those notes are still the heart of the museum. Marsh insists that every label should describe not the object but the repair: who did it, how long it took, and what they used. {3} A child's bicycle, for example, was kept on the road by three generations of the same family, and its label lists every part that has been replaced, along with the name of the person who replaced it. Some labels run to two full pages.

Not every repair in the collection is a skilful one. Some are, frankly, terrible. There is a kitchen chair whose broken leg has been replaced with a rolled-up newspaper wrapped in tape, and a pair of glasses with one arm made from a wooden lolly stick. {4} 'Anyone can admire a perfect repair,' he says. 'I'm more interested in the ones where somebody clearly had no idea what they were doing and did it anyway.'

The museum nearly closed in its second year, when the owner of the building decided to sell. {5} Several of those who gave money now volunteer at the museum, and one of them, a retired nurse called Joan Petty, runs a weekly workshop where visitors bring in broken things and learn to fix them.

The workshop has become so popular that there is now a waiting list. {6} 'People arrive saying they're hopeless with their hands,' she says. 'Most of them have just never been allowed to try.' Her own favourite moment, she adds, is the silence in the room when something that has been dead for years suddenly comes back to life.

Marsh, now eighty-one, still comes in every morning to dust the shelves. Asked which object he would save in a fire, he points without hesitation to a radio with a pencil inside it. 'It doesn't work, of course,' he says. 'It stopped working years ago. But you can see that somebody loved it.'
sentences: When local people heard the news, they raised enough money in six weeks to persuade the new owner to let it stay.
This, he says, is where the real stories are.
Its organiser believes that what most people lack is not skill but confidence.
That is the only thing the objects have in common.
Several of these were mended by Marsh himself, who admits he has never been much good with his hands.
Visitors often laugh at such objects, which does not bother Marsh in the least.
When a neighbour gave him a radio her late husband had mended with a pencil and a hair clip, he put it in his front window with a handwritten label telling its story.
why: 'That' points back to 'was broken once'; the list that follows shows that each object was also repaired.
The neighbour's radio is the 'accident'; a label in his front window explains how 'word had spread'. The pencil radio returns in the last paragraph.
'This' is the repair, not the object; the bicycle with its list of replaced parts is the example of a 'real story'.

'Such objects' are the newspaper chair and the lolly-stick glasses; Marsh's comment explains why the laughter does not bother him. E also follows the terrible repairs, but Marsh spent thirty-five years repairing televisions, so he cannot be bad with his hands.
'The news' is the planned sale; 'those who gave money' in the next sentence are the local people who raised it.
'Its' is the workshop, and 'she says' is the organiser, Joan Petty, explaining the lack of confidence.
